title: Who Really Controls Grant Money
hook: The legislature appropriates the money, but the executive writes the rules for handing it out. A proposed U.S. rule would let officials end a federal grant 'at any time, for any reason.'
key_points: A proposed Office of Management and Budget rule would let agencies terminate federal grants 'at any time, for any reason,' with minimal explanation or appeal.
It would give political appointees discretion over grant decisions regardless of subject-matter expertise, and curb some international research collaborations.
The scope is broad — hundreds of billions of dollars, spanning NSF and NIH research plus food assistance, housing, small-business loans, and the arts.
OMB director Russell Vought had already canceled 284 Department of Energy grants.
An agency lawyer conceded in court those cancellations were 'based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient's state.'
Nearly 500,000 public comments were filed opposing the rule, per ProPublica — notice-and-comment is where a rule like this can still be contested.
content_html: Follow the money in any government and you find two separate powers. One is the power to appropriate — a legislature voting that a sum shall be spent on research, or housing, or food aid. The other is the power to decide who actually gets it, on what conditions, and when it can be taken back. That second power lives in the executive branch, it is exercised through rules rather than laws, and it attracts far less attention.
extra_html:
ProPublica's Lisa Song reports on a rule proposed by the U.S. Office of Management and Budget, directed by Russell Vought, that would sharply expand that second power. Per the reporting, the rule would let agencies terminate grants "at any time, for any reason," with minimal explanation and little opportunity to appeal, and would place grant decisions in the hands of political appointees regardless of whether they have expertise in the subject. It also restricts research collaborations with certain foreign countries. The reach is not limited to science: the rule covers hundreds of billions of dollars in federal grants, from National Science Foundation and National Institutes of Health work on cancer treatment, maternal health, and fundamental physics, to food stamps, housing, small-business loans, and arts funding.

The mechanism already has a track record. Vought's OMB had previously canceled 284 Department of Energy grants, and an agency lawyer acknowledged in court that those cancellations were "based solely on the political identity of the grant recipient's state." University of Chicago physicist David W. Miller, who worked on the Higgs boson discovery, told ProPublica the rule tells scientists that "your funding is safe only as long as your work... remain acceptable to the current administration," warning that "the United States will not just fall behind. It will step aside." Whatever one makes of the specific rule, the general lesson holds across democracies: funding that can be withdrawn at will is a standing instrument of influence over the people who depend on it, and the notice-and-comment stage — which drew nearly 500,000 opposing comments here — is the main point at which outsiders get to push back before such a rule takes effect. (This card describes a U.S. federal rulemaking; the machinery of grant-making differs by country.)

related.title: Strings Attached: When Federal Money Becomes Leverage
related.hook: A national government that can't order regions around directly can often get the same result by attaching conditions to its money — which is why courts ask where persuasion ends and coercion begins.

related.title: Rulemaking Is Supposed to Include the Public — What Happens When It Doesn't
related.hook: Before a federal agency can change a regulation, it's normally required to ask the public first. A 2026 overhaul of grazing rules on federal land tested how easily that step can be trimmed.

related.title: What Happens When a Country Defunds Its Public Broadcaster
related.hook: A year after the U.S. ended six decades of federal support for public media, the stations are still on air — but the mix of who pays for them, and which ones survive, has changed.

flashcards.prompt: Why is control over how a grant is awarded and ended a form of policy power?
flashcards.back_html: A legislature votes the money, but whoever sets the award and termination rules decides who actually receives it — real policy discretion that never requires a new law.

flashcards.prompt: Why would an 'at any time, for any reason' termination clause change a grantee's behavior even if no grant is ever cancelled?

choices.text: Revocable funding creates an ongoing incentive to keep work acceptable to whoever holds the discretion
It requires grantees to reapply for their grant every month
It automatically transfers the grant to a different agency

flashcards.explanation_html: The physicist quoted by ProPublica made exactly this point: the rule signals that funding is safe only as long as the work stays acceptable to the current administration. The leverage lies in its being revocable.

flashcards.prompt: What made the 284 cancelled Department of Energy grants legally notable?

choices.text: An agency lawyer conceded in court they were based solely on the political identity of the recipient's state
A court ruled that grants may never be cancelled once awarded
Congress had explicitly barred that agency from issuing grants

flashcards.explanation_html: The in-court concession is what turns a contested claim into a documented one — an admission that the criterion was political geography rather than the merits of the work.
